# Introduction

This vignette demonstrates how to fit multiple soil depth motif types to soil property data and select the best-fitting model. We'll cover:

- Preparing soil profile data for motif fitting
- Fitting individual motifs with optimization
- Automated model selection across all motif types
- Interpreting and visualizing results

# Data Preparation

Soil motif fitting requires continuous depth profiles. The `sm_prepare()` function handles conversion from discrete horizon data to continuous profiles using different interpolation methods.

```{r data_prep}
# Example horizon data with realistic pedogenic patterns
horizon_data <- data.frame(
  id = c("P1", "P1", "P1", "P1"),
  top = c(0, 15, 45, 90),
  bottom = c(15, 45, 90, 120),
  clay = c(8, 25, 35, 42)  # Clay accumulates with depth (argillic horizon pattern)
)

# Convert to continuous profile
profiles <- sm_prepare(horizon_data, property = "clay", method = "linear")
clay_profile <- profiles$clay$P1

# Plot the profile
depths <- 1:200
plot(clay_profile, depths, ylim = c(200, 1), type = "l",
     xlab = "Clay Content (%)", ylab = "Depth (cm)",
     main = "Prepared Clay Profile (Linear Interpolation)",
     lwd = 2, col = "darkblue")

# Add reference lines for data range
abline(v = range(clay_profile), lty = 3, col = "gray")
cat("Profile clay content range:", range(clay_profile), "\n")
cat("Profile clay content mean:", mean(clay_profile), "\n")
```

# Fitting Individual Motifs

You can fit individual motif types using `sm_optim()`. Each motif type has different parameters:

```{r individual_fits}
# Fit different motif types with better-informed starting parameters
# Initial params should be roughly within the data range [8, 42]
sigmoid_fit <- sm_optim(clay_profile, c(30, 80), FUN = sm_shape_wetting_front)
peak_fit <- sm_optim(clay_profile, c(25, 50), FUN = sm_shape_peak)
gradational_fit <- sm_optim(clay_profile, c(15, 50), FUN = sm_shape_gradational)

# Plot comparisons
plot(clay_profile, depths, ylim = c(200, 1), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Clay Content (%)", ylab = "Depth (cm)",
     main = "Individual Motif Fits")
lines(sigmoid_fit, depths, col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(peak_fit, depths, col = "red", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
lines(gradational_fit, depths, col = "green", lty = 4, lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", 
       c("Observed", "Wetting Front", "Peak", "Gradational"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3, 4), col = c("black", "blue", "red", "green"), lwd = 2)

# Show fitted parameters
cat("Wetting Front (Sigmoid) params:", attr(sigmoid_fit, 'par'), "\n")
cat("Peak params:", attr(peak_fit, 'par'), "\n")
cat("Gradational params:", attr(gradational_fit, 'par'), "\n")
```

# Automated Model Selection

The `fit_motif_auto()` function automatically fits all motif types and ranks them by goodness-of-fit criteria.

```{r auto_selection}
# Automated model selection
results <- fit_motif_auto(clay_profile, criterion = "AIC")
```

# Uncertainty Quantification via Bootstrap

The `sm_optim_bootstrap()` function provides uncertainty estimates for fitted model parameter through bootstrap resampling. The method adapts based on data resolution:

- **Parametric Bootstrap**: For sparse data (observations <= threshold), residuals are resampled from a normal distribution
- **Sieve Bootstrap**: For dense data (observations > threshold), residuals are modeled as an AR(1) process and non-parametrically resampled

```{r bootstrap_basic, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
# Use parametric bootstrap for illustration
# (Sieve bootstrap would be automatically selected for n=200)
set.seed(42)
boot_result <- sm_optim_bootstrap(  
  observed = clay_profile,
  depths = depths,
  initial_params = c(20, 60),  # Appropriate starting values for sigmoid
  shape_family = "sigmoid",
  optimizer = "lbfgs",
  n_bootstrap = 1000,  # Sufficient samples for stable CI estimates
  method = "parametric"  # Explicit method for reproducibility
)

# Examine bootstrap results
cat("Bootstrap samples generated:", boot_result$settings$n_bootstrap, "\n")
cat("Successful fits:", boot_result$n_successful, "\n")
cat("Bootstrap method:", boot_result$method_used, "\n\n")

# Extract parameter estimates and confidence intervals
param_samples <- boot_result$param_samples
param_means <- colMeans(param_samples, na.rm = TRUE)
param_sds <- apply(param_samples, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
param_ci_lower <- apply(param_samples, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
param_ci_upper <- apply(param_samples, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)

# Display results
cat("Parameter Estimates with 95% Confidence Intervals:\n")
for (i in 1:length(param_means)) {
  cat(sprintf("  Param %d: %.2f +/- %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]\n",
              i, param_means[i], param_sds[i], 
              param_ci_lower[i], param_ci_upper[i]))
}

# Visualize bootstrap samples as distribution
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(param_samples[, 1], main = "Distribution of Parameter 1", 
     xlab = "Parameter 1 Value", breaks = 30, col = "skyblue")
hist(param_samples[, 2], main = "Distribution of Parameter 2",
     xlab = "Parameter 2 Value", breaks = 30, col = "lightcoral")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The bootstrap reveals the parameter uncertainty by showing how parameter estimates vary across resampled datasets. **Non-zero confidence interval widths** indicate genuine uncertainty in the fitted parameters, which is valuable for interpreting model results.

## Comparing Bootstrap Methods

You can explicitly compare parametric and sieve bootstrap to assess how residual autocorrelation affects uncertainty. For this comparison, we'll use synthetic data with known moderate autocorrelation:

```{r bootstrap_comparison}
# Create synthetic data with controlled noise and moderate autocorrelation
set.seed(123)
depths_synthetic <- 1:200
# Generate AR(1) process with phi = 0.4 (moderate positive autocorrelation)
phi_true <- 0.4
eps <- rnorm(200, mean = 0, sd = 5)
ar_noise <- numeric(200)
ar_noise[1] <- eps[1]
for (i in 2:200) {
  ar_noise[i] <- phi_true * ar_noise[i-1] + eps[i]
}
# Add to sigmoid shape
true_shape <- sm_shape_sigmoid(depths_synthetic, c(40, 100))
synthetic_obs <- 10 + true_shape * 35 + ar_noise  # 10-45 range with AR noise

# Parametric bootstrap (faster, assumes independent residuals)
set.seed(42)
boot_param <- sm_optim_bootstrap(
  observed = synthetic_obs,
  depths = depths_synthetic,
  initial_params = c(40, 100),
  shape_family = "sigmoid",
  optimizer = "lbfgs",
  n_bootstrap = 500,
  method = "parametric"
)

# Sieve bootstrap (accounts for AR(1) autocorrelation)
set.seed(42)
boot_sieve <- sm_optim_bootstrap(
  observed = synthetic_obs,
  depths = depths_synthetic,
  initial_params = c(40, 100),
  shape_family = "sigmoid",
  optimizer = "lbfgs",
  n_bootstrap = 500,
  method = "sieve"
)

# Compare variability
cat("=== Parameter Uncertainty Comparison (Synthetic Data with AR(1)=0.4) ===\n")
cat("Method           | Param 1 SD | Param 2 SD | AR(1) coef | Notes\n")
cat(sprintf("Parametric       |   %.4f   |   %.4f   | N/A        | Assumes independence\n",
            sd(boot_param$param_samples[, 1], na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(boot_param$param_samples[, 2], na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Sieve            |   %.4f   |   %.4f   | %.4f   | Accounts for AR(1)\n",
            sd(boot_sieve$param_samples[, 1], na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(boot_sieve$param_samples[, 2], na.rm = TRUE),
            if (is.na(boot_sieve$ar1_coef)) NA else boot_sieve$ar1_coef))

# Calculate empirical AR(1) from residuals
fit_syn <- sm_optim(synthetic_obs, c(40, 100), FUN = sm_shape_sigmoid)
residuals_syn <- synthetic_obs - fit_syn
mean_res <- mean(residuals_syn)
centered <- residuals_syn - mean_res
gamma0 <- sum(centered^2) / length(residuals_syn)
gamma1 <- sum(centered[-length(centered)] * centered[-1]) / length(residuals_syn)
ar1_empirical <- gamma1 / gamma0

cat("\nResidual Autocorrelation:\n")
cat("  True AR(1):", phi_true, "\n")
cat("  Empirical AR(1) from residuals:", sprintf("%.4f", ar1_empirical), "\n")
cat("  AR(1) detected by sieve bootstrap:", sprintf("%.4f", boot_sieve$ar1_coef), "\n")

# Show that sieve produces wider confidence intervals when autocorrelation exists
cat("\nDifference in Parameter 1 SD (Sieve - Parametric):",
    sd(boot_sieve$param_samples[, 1], na.rm = TRUE) - 
    sd(boot_param$param_samples[, 1], na.rm = TRUE),
    "(positive means sieve estimates larger uncertainty)\n")
```

**Interpretation**: When residual autocorrelation exists (AR(1) ≠ 0), the sieve bootstrap typically produces wider confidence intervals than parametric bootstrap, because it accounts for the dependency structure in the residuals. The parametric bootstrap may underestimate uncertainty when it ignores autocorrelation.

# Interpreting Results

Different criteria emphasize different aspects of model performance:

- **AIC/BIC**: Balance fit quality with model complexity (prefer lower values)
- **RMSE**: Absolute fit error (prefer lower values)  
- **R^2**: Proportion of variance explained (prefer higher values)

```{r interpretation}
# Compare fit statistics
print(results$stats)

# Best model parameters
best_params <- attr(results$fits[[results$best]], 'par')
cat("Best model:", results$best, "\n")
cat("Parameters:", paste(best_params, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

# Working with Multiple Profiles

You can process multiple soil profiles simultaneously:

```{r multiple_profiles}
# Multiple profiles
multi_data <- data.frame(
  id = c("P1", "P1", "P1", "P2", "P2", "P2"),
  top = c(0, 20, 60, 0, 25, 70),
  bottom = c(20, 60, 100, 25, 70, 120),
  clay = c(12, 28, 38, 8, 22, 45)
)

# Prepare all profiles
all_profiles <- sm_prepare(multi_data, property = "clay", method = "step")

# Fit motifs for each profile
results_list <- lapply(all_profiles$clay, function(profile) {
  fit_motif_auto(profile, criterion = "AIC")
})

# Show results for each profile
for (profile_id in names(results_list)) {
  cat("\nProfile", profile_id, "- Best model:", results_list[[profile_id]]$best, "\n")
}
```

# Advanced Usage

## Custom Objective Functions

You can use different objective functions for optimization:

```{r custom_objective}
# Use sum of squared errors instead of RMSE
custom_fit <- sm_optim(clay_profile, c(50, 100), 
                      FUN = sm_shape_wetting_front,
                      OPTFUN = sm_optim_ssq)
```

## Handling Missing Data

The preprocessing functions handle missing values appropriately:

```{r missing_data}
# Data with missing values
missing_data <- data.frame(
  id = c("P1", "P1", "P1"),
  top = c(0, 30, 70),
  bottom = c(30, 70, 100),
  clay = c(15, NA, 40)  # Missing middle horizon
)

# Linear interpolation will handle the NA
missing_profile <- sm_prepare(missing_data, property = "clay", method = "linear")$clay$P1
plot(missing_profile, depths, ylim = c(200, 1), type = "l",
     main = "Profile with Missing Data (Linear Interpolation)")
```

This vignette covers the core workflow for soil motif analysis. For more details on specific motif types and their pedogenic interpretations, see the individual function documentation.
